newsitem.title: GERMANY: Issing says Buba must bring stable mark into EMU.
newsitem.headline: Issing says Buba must bring stable mark into EMU.

text.p: Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said on Thursday that the central bank had a duty to bring the deutschemark into European economic and monetary union (EMU) as a stable currency.

In a transcript of a television interview due to be broadcast later on Thursday on Germany's N-TV channel, Issing also said that there was "no need for panic" in the face of Germany's bullish stock market.
Germany's stock market has gained almost 50 percent since the beginning of the year, with the DAX leading share index hitting repeated fresh record highs in recent weeks.

Looking at M3 money supply, which the Bundesbank targets as an early indicator of inflationary pressure when setting its monetary policy, Issing said that while M3 had hit the central bank's target corridor in June, this did not mean M3 growth should no longer be a concern.
M3 money supply growth slowed to 6.4 percent in June from 7.0 percent in May -- coming just within the Bundesbank's 3.5 to 6.5 percent target corridor for the first time this year.
"(That is) no reason to stop worrying," the transcript quoted Issing as saying. "For stability, we need a further slowing of (M3) growth."
N-TV's report said Issing said the question was whether the Bundesbank would need to take measures in the future if money supply growth did not continue to fall on its own.

The transcript also said Issing had voiced concern about the speed and size of the recent decline of the mark against the dollar, adding that the Bundesbank would continue keep a close eye on the value of the German currency.
The mark sank to a six-year low against the dollar at 1.84 marks on Thursday, but later recovered slightly and was trading at 1.8346 by 1904 GMT.
The Bundesbank's task was "to bring the mark into monetary union in a stable form and present the European Central Bank (ECB) with a stable environment," Issing said.
He added that the ECB would have a tough enough job as it was, without having to correct earlier monetary policy mistakes made by national central banks, the transcript said.
The ECB is due to come into being 1998 and will take over contol of European monetary policy in the euro area with the scheduled launch of the single currency in January 1999.
